original_summary: Red7 is a card-shedding survival game. Each turn a player adds a card to their face-up palette and/or changes the rule card that decides who is 'winning', and must be winning after their turn or be eliminated. The last player standing wins the hand. The reviewed variation, Red3, cut it to 21 cards, 3 colours, 3 rules and a points match to 6.

review.evidence: The card play in Red3 holds up against simple policies. Always-fold loses every hand. Always-play-strongest-and-never-switch loses to a rule switch: P has 7V (Red key 71) against Q's 2G, Q discards a Green card and leads 122 to 0. Always option (c) burns two cards a turn and runs out first. The leader is fixed by the dealt card, not the seat. The flaw is the 2-player scoring. Survivor 2 and last-eliminated 1 means the gap is just hands won minus hands lost, so every 2-2 split ends 6-6. That draws about 37% of matches between equals and about 35% at p=0.6.

Within a hand, card conservation and timing of rule switches decide survival, so skill shows. Over a 2-player match, though, a third of results are draws whatever the skill gap. At p=0.6 the stronger player wins only about 45% of matches outright. Each individual hand also carries real deal luck: the dealt palette fixes the first leader and the 5-card hand matters.

Strong play involves several things: holding high cards back, inferring opponents' hands from the unseen cards (21 cards, at most 18 dealt), switching to a rule the opponent cannot answer, and keeping enough cards to outlast them. A weak player still wins some hands through the deal.

Hands and the set-aside cards are hidden. Whether a switch to Green is safe depends on whether the opponent likely holds an even card that beats your key. That must be inferred from the cards visible in palettes and on the canvas, and from how the opponent has chosen to spend cards so far.
Keys are arithmetic on public palette cards, eliminations are mechanical and points are counted. No judgement is needed.

The game is turn-based text with hidden hands, one shuffle per hand and a 40-round cap. Each turn costs at least one card, so a hand lasts at most 6 rounds. The 21-card deck supports 2 or 3 players: 4 players would need 24 dealt cards, which the original's '2 to 4' cannot cover.

problems: In 2 players the 2/1 hand scoring makes the score gap equal hands won minus hands lost, so any 2-2 split reaches 6-6 and the match is a draw (about 35-37% of matches).
The 1-point consolation is meaningless in 2 players, because the loser of a hand is always the last eliminated.
In 3 players a tie for most points at or above 6 (for example a hand winner going 4 to 6 while the runner-up goes 5 to 6) ends in a draw, and a tie at the round-40 cap also gives no winner.
The stated player range must match the deck: 4 players cannot be dealt from 21 cards.

changes.what: In 2-player matches, a hand winner scores 1 point and the loser 0. The first player to 3 points wins (best of five hands).
changes.why: An odd number of hands is needed to decide, so 2-2 can never end the match. A fifth hand always settles it, and the useless consolation point disappears.
changes.fixes: In 2 players the 2/1 hand scoring makes the score gap equal hands won minus hands lost, so any 2-2 split reaches 6-6 and the match is a draw (about 35-37% of matches).

changes.what: The 1-point consolation for the last-eliminated player applies only in 3-player matches.
changes.why: Finishing order genuinely varies in 3 players and is worth fighting for there. In 2 players it adds nothing.
changes.fixes: The 1-point consolation is meaningless in 2 players, because the loser of a hand is always the last eliminated.

changes.what: In 3 players, a tie for most points is broken in favour of the tied player who won the most recently completed hand. This applies both at the 6-point end and at the round-40 cap.
changes.why: Each hand has exactly one survivor, so 'most recent hand winner' always picks out one player. It also rewards closing out the deciding hand.
changes.fixes: In 3 players a tie for most points at or above 6 (for example a hand winner going 4 to 6 while the runner-up goes 5 to 6) ends in a draw, and a tie at the round-40 cap also gives no winner.

changes.what: The player count is fixed at 2 or 3.
changes.why: The deal of 5 hidden cards plus 1 palette card per player needs 12 or 18 of the 21 cards. That always leaves some cards unseen, which keeps inference alive.
changes.fixes: The stated player range must match the deck: 4 players cannot be dealt from 21 cards.

keeps: Must be leading at the end of your own turn or be eliminated.
Value beats colour: strength = number x 10 + colour rank.
Discarding to the Canvas changes the rule, and play-then-discard is allowed.
Three of Red7's rules: highest card, most evens, most cards below 4.
Hidden hands, public palettes, last player standing wins the hand.
A multi-hand match scored by hands survived.

recommendation.reason: The card play already rewards inference and planning. Only the match-scoring structure produced draws, and that is fixed with arithmetic winner rules inside the limits.

variation.name: Red3 Duel
variation.summary: A 21-card, 3-colour Red7 for 2 or 3 players. You must lead under the current rule after your own turn, and you may change the rule by discarding. The match is first to 3 hands in a duel, or first to 6 points with a recent-winner tiebreak in 3 players, so every match has a winner.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 21 cards: numbers 1 to 7 in each of three colours, Red, Green and Violet. Colour rank is Red 3, Green 2, Violet 1. A card's strength is number x 10 + colour rank (7 Red = 73, 4 Violet = 41). Higher strength beats lower. A card is EVEN if its number is 2, 4 or 6. A card is LOW if its number is 1, 2 or 3.

THE RULE. The Canvas shows one colour, which is the current rule. Each living player has a KEY under the current rule:
- Red: key = strength of the highest card in your palette.
- Green: key = 100 x (number of even cards in your palette) + strength of your highest even card, or 0 if you have no even card.
- Violet: key = 100 x (number of low cards in your palette) + strength of your highest low card, or 0 if you have no low card.
You are LEADING if your key is strictly higher than every other living player's key. If keys tie, including at 0, no tied player is leading.

SETUP OF A HAND. Shuffle all 21 cards. Deal each player 5 cards as a hidden hand, then 1 card face up as their palette. The remaining cards (9 with 2 players, 3 with 3 players) are set aside unseen for this hand. The Canvas starts as Red. Everyone is alive. The initial leader is the player whose palette card has the highest strength. The first turn of the hand goes to the next player in seat order after that leader.

A TURN. On your turn choose exactly one:
(a) play one card from your hand face up to your palette;
(b) discard one card from your hand to the Canvas, so the rule becomes that card's colour and the card leaves play;
(c) do (a), then (b), with two different cards;
(d) fold.
Then recompute keys under the current rule. If you are not leading, or you folded, or you named a card you do not hold, you are eliminated. Your palette stays visible but no longer counts. If you have no cards left in hand when your turn comes, you can only fold. Play passes to the next living player in seat order.

A ROUND is one pass of turns through all living players in seat order, starting with the player whose turn it is.

END OF A HAND. A hand ends the moment only one player is alive. That player is the hand winner.
- With 2 players: the hand winner scores 1 point; the other scores 0.
- With 3 players: the hand winner scores 2 points; the player whose elimination left one survivor scores 1; the first player eliminated scores 0.
The engine records the hand winner as the MOST RECENT HAND WINNER. If the match is not over, a new hand is set up at the start of the next round.

END OF THE MATCH.
- With 2 players, the match ends when a player reaches 3 points.
- With 3 players, the match ends after any hand in which a player reaches 6 or more points.
- In either case, it also ends when round 40 is complete; an unfinished hand then scores nothing.

INFORMATION. Palettes, the Canvas, eliminations, points and the most recent hand winner are public. Hands and set-aside cards are hidden. There is no table talk.
variation.objective: The player with the most points when the match ends wins. With 2 players this is the first to 3 points, and a tie cannot occur at that end. If two or more players share the most points, which can happen in 3 players or at the round-40 cap, the tied player who won the most recently completed hand wins. If no hand was completed at all, the match is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Draws in 2-player matches go from about 35% to essentially 0. With p=0.6 per hand, the stronger player now wins the best of five about 68% of the time instead of about 45% outright. Every hand matters to the end, and hand 5 is a true decider. In 3 players the recent-winner tiebreak removes draws and makes winning the deciding hand worth more than limping into second. Talk is left out: play is sequential and hidden-hand inference is the core skill, so cheap, unenforceable claims would add steps without adding a real decision. Within a hand, play is unchanged: players weigh when to spend high cards, infer from visible and discarded cards what opponents can answer, and switch rules to strand them.

balanced.evidence: WINNER RULE CHECK, 2 players. Each hand gives the survivor 2 points and the other player 1, because the last eliminated player is always the loser. After k hands, if A has won a of them, the scores are A = k + a and B = 2k - a. So the score gap is simply hands won minus hands lost. No one can reach 6 points before hand 3. k=3 with a=3 or a=0 is a sweep, 6-3, and the match is decided. k=3 with a=1 or a=2 gives 4-5 or 5-4, so a 4th hand is played. In hand 4, a=3 gives 7-5 and a=1 gives 5-7, both decided. a=2 gives 6-6, a DRAW. Between equal players (p=0.5 per hand): P(sweep) = 2 x 1/8 = 0.25 and P(2-1 split) = 0.75. The 4th hand then draws whenever the trailing player wins it, so P(draw) = 0.75 x 0.5 = 0.375. With p=0.6 for the stronger player: P(sweep) = 0.216 + 0.064 = 0.28. P(strong leads 2-1) = 0.432, then a draw with probability 0.4, giving 0.173. P(weak leads 2-1) = 0.288, then a draw with probability 0.6, giving 0.173. So P(draw) is about 0.35. In 2 players the 1-point consolation does nothing except force a draw on every 2-2 split, so about a third of matches have no winner. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES: Always fold: eliminated on the first turn of every hand, scoring 1 against 2 each hand, so it always loses. Always play your strongest card under the current rule and never switch: it wastes high cards, and an opponent who switches the rule eliminates it (example below). It does not win or draw almost always. Always option (c): it burns two cards per turn. In an attrition game where each turn costs at least one card, it runs out first and loses. NO DOMINANT OPTION. Example: P's palette is 7V (Red key 71) and Q's is 2G. Q can discard a Green card to make the rule Green, giving Q a key of 122 against P's 0. P can answer by playing 6R, for a Green key of 163. Rule switches and card conservation are real trade-offs. SEAT AND ORDER: the non-leader acts first and spends cards first, so the leader has some tempo. But the leader is set by the dealt palette card, not by seat, so no seat has a fixed edge. In 3 players the 2/1/0 split rewards finishing order and works. The failure is the 2-player draw structure.

playable.evidence: RULES ARE COMPLETE. Keys are defined arithmetically for all three rules. Having no even or low card gives key 0, and 0 against 0 is not strictly higher, so neither player leads. Distinct non-zero keys are guaranteed because the card that sets each player's key is unique. Fold, naming a card you do not hold, an empty hand (only fold is possible) and end-of-hand scoring are all covered. Playing a card never lowers a key under any rule. So a player who is already leading at the start of their turn, which can happen in 3 players after another player's rule change and elimination, can always play a card and stay alive. The rules handle this. FINITENESS: each turn spends at least one card from a 5-card hand, so a hand lasts at most about 5 rounds. A 2-player match lasts at most 4 hands (about 20 rounds). A 3-player match is also well under the 40-round cap. LIMITS: steps 18 <= 20 (tight: about 5 per turn x 3 seats, plus scoring, redeal and the match check). Choice steps 3 <= 4: one per seat, and option (c) names two cards in one choice. Attributes 14 <= 20. Hidden elements 2 <= 3. Random draws: 1 per round, the shuffle at hand setup. Rounds 40 <= 40. The leading check is pure arithmetic. Turns are sequential, which is correct for this game. TALK: no table talk in 3 players is sensible. All actions and palettes are public and sequential, and no proposal could be enforced, so players reason from the visible state rather than guessing. No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed. This is not a repeated cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: CHANCE: the 5-card deal and the leader's tempo, with 6 to 9 of the 21 cards set aside. I estimate the deal decides roughly 40-50% of single hands. A match of 3 or 4 hands dilutes this. SKILL: choosing between playing a card and switching the rule, and which rule to switch to. Conserving cards so the opponent runs out of answers first. Avoiding option (c), which spends two cards. Inferring the opponent's hand from the rules they avoid and the cards they hold back. In the 7V/2G example, a Green or Violet switch overturns a Red lead built on one high card. So under good play the deal alone does not decide the result: a strong Red hand can be neutralised. Inference is moderate rather than deep, because the opponent's hand comes from many unseen cards. Still, it gives a clear edge to the player who reasons well.

required_changes: Fix the 2-player draw structure. Option 1: in 2 players the hand winner scores 1 point, the loser scores 0, and the match goes to the first player with 3 points, so the match can never end on a 2-2 tie. Option 2: keep the 6-point target but break a tie for the most points in favour of the player who won the most recent hand.

balanced.evidence: SCORING TABLE PER HAND: with 2 players the winner gets 1 and the loser 0. With 3 players the winner gets 2, the second player out gets 1 and the first out gets 0, so 3 points are handed out per hand. KEY RANGES: strength runs from 11 (1 Violet) to 73 (7 Red), and all 21 strengths are distinct. A Red key can therefore never tie, because every palette holds at least 1 card. Under Green and Violet, the 100x count term (100-300+) always outweighs the highest-card term (at most 73). So the keys are lexicographic, as intended, and the arithmetic is consistent. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE: (1) Always fold. You are eliminated on your first turn and lose every hand against any opponent, so the 2p match goes 0-3. (2) Always (a), play your highest card, never change the rule. Under Red this works only while your top card outranks the opponent's palette. A sensible opponent answers with (b), discarding a Green or Violet card to switch to a rule where their palette has more evens or lows. The greedy player must then match that even or low count, which their high cards may not do, and their high cards are already spent, so they lose often. Against a random opponent it usually wins, because a random named move is often illegal or non-leading and eliminates that player. It does not win almost every time against sensible play. (3) Always (c), play then discard. This burns 2 cards per turn and empties a 5-card hand in 3 turns, after which you are forced to fold. It loses to an opponent who conserves cards. (4) Always (b) to the same colour. If the rule already matches, this only spends cards. You lead only if your palette already wins, so it is no better than doing nothing. NO STRICTLY DOMINANT OPTION: whether (a), (b) or (c) is right depends on both palettes, the canvas and the cards held. Folding is weakly dominated, except when nothing can make you lead, where all options are equivalent. SEAT AND ORDER: the initial leader and the first mover are set by the deal (highest palette strength), not by a fixed seat. The first mover must spend a card to overtake, then the leader must respond. As in Red7, this is a deal-dependent tension, not a seat edge, and it falls randomly to each seat. Information is symmetric: every player sees all palettes and holds a hidden 5-card hand. Both players can realistically win any hand and the match.

playable.evidence: COMPLETENESS: the rules cover the deck, strength, EVEN and LOW, the three keys (including the 0 case), strict leading with ties (no tied player is leading), setup, the four turn options, the elimination triggers (not leading, fold, naming a card not held), the empty-hand forced fold, turn order, the round definition, the hand end, scoring for 2p and 3p, the match end, the round-40 cap, and tie-breaks (most recent hand winner, else draw). FINITENESS: every non-fold turn uses at least 1 card from a 5-card hand. Each player therefore takes at most 5 card-turns plus 1 forced fold, so a hand lasts at most about 6 rounds. 2p: first to 3 points means at most 5 hands, and 5 x 6 = 30 rounds, under 40. 3p: rotating results can stretch the match, but the round-40 cap (the unfinished hand scores nothing) and the defined tie-break keep it finite. LIMITS: steps per round. Conditional hand setup (shuffle, deal, palettes, canvas, alive flags, leader and first turn) takes about 4 steps, each with a `when` condition, so no conditional block is needed. Each turn takes 1 sequential choice, 1 card move, and 1 key recompute plus leading check (arithmetic via calc, or a referee check on the palette). For 3 players that is about 9 steps, plus about 2 for scoring and match end, roughly 15 in total, within 20. Choice steps: 3, within 4. Attributes: 13, within 20. Hidden elements: 2 (hands and set-aside cards), within 3. Random draws: 1 shuffle in a round where a hand starts, within 1. Rounds: 40, within 40. No board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed. Sequential choice is correct because turns genuinely happen in order. TALK: the 3p game has no talk, which is sensible. Moves are sequential and all palettes are public, so players never have to guess a simultaneous action, and talk would mainly add kingmaking chatter. REPEATED-GAME TEST: this is not a cooperation dilemma, and no 'safe option' wins late rounds; folding always loses.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: WHAT DECIDES A HAND: the deal sets resources, but Red7-style play rewards three skills. First, conserving cards: lead by the smallest margin and keep high, even and low cards for later. Second, timing rule switches to a colour where your palette dominates. Third, inferring the opponent's hand. In 2p you see 6 of 21 cards plus both palettes; 15 are unknown, 5 of them in the opponent's hand. Plays and discards reveal more as the hand goes on. In 3p only 3 cards are set aside, so deduction is sharp. CHANCE ESTIMATE: a single hand is perhaps 40-50% decided by the deal. The 2p match is first to 3 hands and 3p needs 6 points over several hands, which cuts the share of match results decided by chance alone to roughly 25-35%. ALL PLAYERS PLAYING WELL: outcomes still turn on reading hidden hands and on who misjudges when to switch rules. Hidden information means play is not fully determined, so the result is not decided by the random draw alone. A skilled player clearly beats a greedy or random one, as policies (2)-(4) above show.
